extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in the history and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and extract G. H. Hardy's criteria and standards for judging the value and beauty of mathematical work as presented in A Mathematician's Apology (1940). Emphasizes aesthetic, originality, purity, and related evaluative principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics has value independent of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy argues that mathematics has value independent of its applications; the central justification for mathematics is its beauty rather than utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy locates mathematical value in beauty (compare to painting and poetry) and explicitly defends pursuing mathematics 'for its own sake' rather than for applied uses. This is the primary evaluative stance of the Apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for pure mathematics (especially number theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The most beautiful mathematics was that which had no practical applications (pure mathematics) and, in particular, number theory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy singles out pure mathematics — and number theory in particular — as the highest form, because its concepts are deeper and more elegant. He treats apparent 'uselessness' as a mark (and justification) of high mathematical beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uselessness as a virtue / safeguard against harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy's claim: the 'uselessness' of much higher mathematics is a positive feature because it means the mathematics 'cannot be misused to cause harm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This moral/ethical argument is used to justify pure mathematics: lack of practical application is presented as preventing destructive uses (e.g., war technology). This is an explicit evaluative criterion in Hardy's defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality: doing mathematics means proving new theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The function of a mathematician is to do something, to prove new theorems, to add to mathematics, and not to talk about what he or other mathematicians have done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy values creative, original work (new theorems, advances) over exposition, criticism, or appreciation. He treats original contribution as the core standard of mathematical worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and depth of underlying concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy (citing Gauss) values the relative 'depth' and 'elegance' of underlying concepts as a measure of mathematical preeminence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He contrasts deep, elegant theories (e.g., Galois-style mathematics) with more elementary results (e.g., Rolle's theorem) to illustrate that elegance and conceptual depth are key evaluative criteria for 'real' mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applied mathematics criticised for simplicity, vulgarity, and dullness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy denigrates much applied mathematics as 'trivial', 'ugly', or 'dull', contrasting it with 'real mathematics' (pure mathematics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses a negative evaluative standard: mathematical work that is primarily applied, routine, or lacking elegance is judged inferior. The article also notes Hardy's view is based on aesthetic judgments (simplicity/vulgarity) rather than mere applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a 'young man's game' (age-related expectation of creativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy's thesis that mathematics is a 'young man's game' — talent for producing original mathematics tends to belong to the young, and creativity declines with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both autobiographical and prescriptive: the timing of one's most valuable creative contributions (early in life) is treated as an implicit standard for evaluating careers/works (originality produced while young is prized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition/criticism regarded as second-rate work
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy's claim: 'Exposition, criticism, appreciation, is work for second-rate minds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This places low value on expository or critical work compared to original research; thus evaluating mathematical work downweights exposition-heavy contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: dismissing applied work because no current application (historical critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique: Hardy's confident assertion that number theory and relativity had no warlike purpose proved mistaken (e.g., Enigma codebreaking, public-key cryptography, nuclear weapons), showing a danger in dismissing applied potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses Hardy's later-demonstrated errors as a caution: using present lack of application as a criterion for aesthetic or moral superiority can be misleading. This functions as negative guidance/anti-pattern to Hardy's explicit standards.
